title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
text:
In 2010, Steyerberg, Vickers, Cook, Gerds, Gonen, Obuchowski, Pencina, and Kattan published a useful framework for thinking about prediction-model performance: do not reduce model evaluation to a single number.
Their paper, Assessing the Performance of Prediction Models: A Framework for Traditional and Novel Measures, discusses several families of performance measures. The core message is still highly practical: discrimination and calibration answer different questions, and decision-analytic measures are needed when predictions will actually be used to make decisions.
This post translates that workflow into a compact Python example with rtichoke.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
text:
Setup
We will compare two logistic-regression models for predicting malignant breast cancer. The first deliberately uses only two predictors; the second uses the full feature set.

import numpy as np

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from rtichoke import (
    create_calibration_curve,
    create_decision_curve,
    create_roc_curve,
)


data = load_breast_cancer()
X = data.data

# sklearn encodes malignant as 0 and benign as 1.
# Flip the target so that the event of interest is malignancy.
y = 1 - data.target

X_train, X_valid, y_train, y_valid = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=2026,
    stratify=y,
)

baseline_columns = [0, 1]  # mean radius, mean texture

baseline_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=2_000),
)
full_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=2_000),
)

baseline_model.fit(X_train[:, baseline_columns], y_train)
full_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

baseline_prob = baseline_model.predict_proba(
    X_valid[:, baseline_columns]
)[:, 1]
full_prob = full_model.predict_proba(X_valid)[:, 1]

probs = {
    "Baseline model": baseline_prob,
    "Full model": full_prob,
}

The important object for the rest of the analysis is simply a dictionary of predicted probabilities plus the observed binary outcomes. rtichoke does not care how those predictions were produced.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
text:
1. Overall performance
Steyerberg et al. discuss the Brier score as an overall measure of prediction error. Lower is better, with perfect probabilistic predictions reaching zero.

for name, p in probs.items():
    print(
        f"{name}: "
        f"AUC={roc_auc_score(y_valid, p):.3f}, "
        f"Brier={brier_score_loss(y_valid, p):.3f}"
    )

Baseline model: AUC=0.940, Brier=0.093
Full model: AUC=0.987, Brier=0.030


A summary statistic is useful, but it does not tell us why one set of predictions is better than another. That is where the decomposition into discrimination, calibration, and utility becomes useful.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
section: 2. Discrimination: can the model rank patients?
text:
2. Discrimination: can the model rank patients?
The ROC curve asks how well predictions separate patients with and without the outcome across thresholds. The area under the curve is a ranking measure: it does not tell us whether a predicted risk of 30% really means a 30% event probability.

create_roc_curve(
    probs=probs,
    reals=y_valid,
)

                                                


This is why a high AUC is not a complete model evaluation. A model can rank patients well while producing probabilities that are systematically too high or too low.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
section: 3. Calibration: do the probabilities mean what they say?
text:
3. Calibration: do the probabilities mean what they say?
Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed outcome frequencies. This is a different property from discrimination and should be inspected directly.

create_calibration_curve(
    probs=probs,
    reals=y_valid,
    calibration_type="smooth",
)

                                                


The histogram under the calibration curve is useful here: it shows where the predictions actually live. Calibration behavior in a region with almost no patients should not be interpreted in the same way as calibration where predictions are dense.
A useful mental model is:

Discrimination: who is at higher risk?
Calibration: how much risk?

Those are related questions, but they are not interchangeable.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
section: 4. Clinical utility: should we act on the predictions?
text:
4. Clinical utility: should we act on the predictions?
The paper also emphasizes decision-analytic measures when a model is intended to guide clinical decisions. Decision curve analysis expresses performance as net benefit across threshold probabilities.
Suppose a clinician would act when predicted malignancy risk exceeds some threshold. Different thresholds encode different relative costs of false-positive and false-negative decisions.

create_decision_curve(
    probs=probs,
    reals=y_valid,
    min_p_threshold=0.01,
    max_p_threshold=0.50,
)

                                                


This plot answers a question that neither AUC nor calibration answers directly:

Over the range of thresholds that matter for the decision, does using the model produce more benefit than default strategies?

A model can therefore have attractive discrimination and still offer little clinical value at the thresholds that matter in practice.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
section: 5. The same decision curve as interventions avoided
text:
5. The same decision curve as interventions avoided
Net benefit is compact but can feel abstract. rtichoke can show the same decision problem using the interventions-avoided representation.

create_decision_curve(
    probs=probs,
    reals=y_valid,
    decision_type="interventions avoided",
    min_p_threshold=0.01,
    max_p_threshold=0.50,
)

                                                


This is often easier to communicate: instead of asking only whether the model has positive net benefit, we can ask how many unnecessary interventions could be avoided while preserving the decision-theoretic trade-off represented by the threshold.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
text:
A practical evaluation sequence
The Steyerberg framework suggests a useful order for model evaluation:

Overall performance gives a compact summary of prediction error.
Discrimination asks whether the model separates higher-risk from lower-risk patients.
Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities are numerically trustworthy.
Clinical utility asks whether acting on those predictions improves decisions.

The important point is not that every project needs every possible metric. It is that each metric answers a different question.
For rtichoke, that leads to a deliberately simple workflow:

create_roc_curve(probs=probs, reals=y_valid)
create_calibration_curve(probs=probs, reals=y_valid)
create_decision_curve(probs=probs, reals=y_valid)

Fit the model however you want. Then evaluate the predictions from several complementary perspectives.

title: Beyond the AUC: the Steyerberg framework in Python
text:
Reference
Steyerberg EW, Vickers AJ, Cook NR, Gerds T, Gonen M, Obuchowski N, Pencina MJ, Kattan MW. Assessing the performance of prediction models: a framework for traditional and novel measures. Epidemiology. 2010;21(1):128-138. DOI: 10.1097/EDE.0b013e3181c30fb2.

title: AGENTS.md
text:
This document outlines the standards and conventions for creating and maintaining this Quarto blog. Following these guidelines will ensure consistency, improve search engine optimization (SEO), and streamline the content creation process.


Each new blog post must be contained within its own subdirectory inside the posts/ directory. The subdirectory name should be a shortened, URL-friendly version of the post’s title (e.g., using-r-with-quarto).
Each post subdirectory must contain an index.qmd file, which will serve as the main content file for the post. Any images or other assets associated with the post should be placed in the same subdirectory.



The following metadata fields are required in the YAML front matter of each index.qmd file:

title: The title of the blog post.
author: The name of the author.
date: The date the post was published, in YYYY-MM-DD format.
description: A brief, one-sentence summary of the post’s content. This is crucial for SEO, as it will be used as the meta description for the page.
categories: A list of relevant categories for the post.



---
title: "My New Blog Post"
author: "John Doe"
date: "2024-01-01"
description: "This is a brief summary of my new blog post."
categories:
  - R
  - Quarto
  - Data Science
---

title: Decision Curves with Fixed Time Horizons
text: rtichoke for Python introduces support for fixed time horizons, allowing flexible specification of the prediction horizon and automatically updating performance plots accordingly.

title: Decision Curves with Fixed Time Horizons
section: The most under-discussed design choice in prediction models: The Time Horizon
text:
The most under-discussed design choice in prediction models: The Time Horizon
Prediction models require a well-defined fixed time horizon: The end of follow-up over which the outcome probability is defined. A probability of dying within 1 week, 1 year, or 100 years represents fundamentally different clinical questions and very different implied decision contexts.
It is therefore important to explore the sensitivity of model performance to the choice of time horizon: Shorter horizons typically yield fewer observed events, resulting in smaller gaps between the two baseline strategies “treat all” (Everyone is considered Predicted Positive) and “treat none” (everyone is considered Predicted Negative).
In contrast, longer horizons may introduce ambiguity through censoring (loss to follow-up) or competing events (events that preclude the primary outcome).

title: Decision Curves with Fixed Time Horizons
section: Pragmatic approach: Performance Sensitivity Analysis with rtichoke
text:
Pragmatic approach: Performance Sensitivity Analysis with rtichoke
You do not need to develop a new or more complex model to overcome these problems, first you need to ensure if there’s a problem at all and for which time horizons:
You can reuse predictions trained for a specific horizon and evaluate their robustness across alternative fixed time horizons: This allows you to assess how performance changes as the effective follow-up window varies without retraining the model.

title: Decision Curves with Fixed Time Horizons
section: Load data and fit a Cox Regression
text:
Load data and fit a Cox Regression

import pandas as pd
import lifelines

df_time_to_cancer_dx = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ddsjoberg/dca-tutorial/main/data/df_time_to_cancer_dx.csv"
)

cph = lifelines.CoxPHFitter()
cph.fit(
    df=df_time_to_cancer_dx,
    duration_col="ttcancer",
    event_col="cancer",
    formula="age + famhistory + marker",
)

cph_pred_vals = cph.predict_survival_function(
    df_time_to_cancer_dx[["age", "famhistory", "marker"]], times=[1.5]
)

df_time_to_cancer_dx["pr_failure18"] = [1 - val for val in cph_pred_vals.iloc[0, :]]

title: Decision Curves with Fixed Time Horizons
section: Decision Curve with Multiple Fixed Time Horizons
text:
Decision Curve with Multiple Fixed Time Horizons
The fixed_time_horizons argument allows you to explicitly define the set of follow-up horizons to evaluate.

from rtichoke import create_decision_curve_times

create_decision_curve_times(
    probs={"full": df_time_to_cancer_dx["pr_failure18"]},
    reals=df_time_to_cancer_dx["cancer"],
    times=df_time_to_cancer_dx["ttcancer"],
    fixed_time_horizons=[0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0]
)

title: Calibration Curves for Multiple Models
text: The following example is inspired by the scikit-learn documentation displaying a calibration curve.

title: Calibration Curves for Multiple Models
text:
Load data and fit models

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=10_000, n_features=20, n_informative=2, n_redundant=10, random_state=42
)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.99, random_state=42
)

lr = LogisticRegression(C=1.0)
gnb = GaussianNB()
gnb_isotonic = CalibratedClassifierCV(gnb, cv=2, method="isotonic")
gnb_sigmoid = CalibratedClassifierCV(gnb, cv=2, method="sigmoid")

lr.fit(X_train, y_train)
gnb.fit(X_train, y_train)
gnb_isotonic.fit(X_train, y_train)
gnb_sigmoid.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_proba_lr = lr.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_proba_gnb = gnb.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_proba_gnb_isotonic = gnb_isotonic.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_proba_gnb_sigmoid = gnb_sigmoid.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

class NaivelyCalibratedLinearSVC(LinearSVC):

    def fit(self, X, y):
        super().fit(X, y)
        df = self.decision_function(X)
        self.df_min_ = df.min()
        self.df_max_ = df.max()

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        df = self.decision_function(X)
        calibrated_df = (df - self.df_min_) / (self.df_max_ - self.df_min_)
        proba_pos_class = np.clip(calibrated_df, 0, 1)
        proba_neg_class = 1 - proba_pos_class
        proba = np.c_[proba_neg_class, proba_pos_class]
        return proba

svc = NaivelyCalibratedLinearSVC(max_iter=10_000)
svc_isotonic = CalibratedClassifierCV(svc, cv=2, method="isotonic")
svc_sigmoid = CalibratedClassifierCV(svc, cv=2, method="sigmoid")

svc.fit(X_train, y_train)
svc_isotonic.fit(X_train, y_train)
svc_sigmoid.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_proba_svc = svc.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_proba_svc_isotonic = svc_isotonic.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_proba_svc_sigmoid = svc_sigmoid.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

title: Calibration Curves for Multiple Models
text:
Gaussian Naive Bayes

rtichokescikit-learn



from rtichoke import create_calibration_curve

create_calibration_curve(
    probs={
        "Logistic": y_proba_lr,
        "Naive Bayes": y_proba_gnb,
        "Naive Bayes + Isotonic": y_proba_gnb_isotonic,
        "Naive Bayes + Sigmoid": y_proba_gnb_sigmoid,
    },
    reals=y_test
).show(config={"displayModeBar": False, "displaylogo": False})

                                                





import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.gridspec import GridSpec
from sklearn.calibration import CalibrationDisplay

clf_list = [
    (lr, "Logistic"),
    (gnb, "Naive Bayes"),
    (gnb_isotonic, "Naive Bayes + Isotonic"),
    (gnb_sigmoid, "Naive Bayes + Sigmoid"),
]

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))
gs = GridSpec(4, 2)
colors = plt.get_cmap("Dark2")

ax_calibration_curve = fig.add_subplot(gs[:2, :2])
calibration_displays = {}
for i, (clf, name) in enumerate(clf_list):
    display = CalibrationDisplay.from_estimator(
        clf,
        X_test,
        y_test,
        n_bins=10,
        name=name,
        ax=ax_calibration_curve,
        color=colors(i),
    )
    calibration_displays[name] = display

ax_calibration_curve.grid()
ax_calibration_curve.set_title("Calibration plots (Naive Bayes)")

grid_positions = [(2, 0), (2, 1), (3, 0), (3, 1)]
for i, (_, name) in enumerate(clf_list):
    row, col = grid_positions[i]
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[row, col])

    ax.hist(
        calibration_displays[name].y_prob,
        range=(0, 1),
        bins=10,
        label=name,
        color=colors(i),
    )
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Mean predicted probability", ylabel="Count")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
